tagline: A winding highway through lake country links Minnesota’s logging stories.
intro: Edge of the Wilderness follows Highway 38 for 47 miles between Effie and Grand Rapids, through pine and hardwood forest, lakes and rolling hills. The Federal Highway Administration identifies this winding road as a National Scenic Byway and recommends three hours to visit its length. Its description singles out lakes, swamps and the fall colors of sugar maple, oak, aspen and birch. Highway 38 passes lake resort areas including Wabana Lake and Trout Lake, and runs through Chippewa National Forest between Bigfork and Itasca County Road 19.

Explore Minnesota describes an earlier route used by voyageurs and loggers through this forest country. The numbered highway came later: Highway 38 was authorized in 1933 and fully paved by 1940. Rail connections had already shaped the towns: Bigfork gained a Minneapolis and Rainy River Railway station in 1906, while Marcell moved its town center closer to the railway in 1910.

Driving south from Effie, reach Bigfork and the side trip to Scenic State Park, seven miles east of Highway 38. Continue through Marcell in the Chippewa National Forest, then finish at Grand Rapids, where the Forest History Center reconstructs a logging camp of 1900. There, the highway meets US 2 in downtown Grand Rapids.

moments.title: Scenic State Park
moments.text: Virgin pine forest surrounds Sandwick and Coon lakes at Scenic State Park, seven miles east of Highway 38 at Bigfork. The park was established in 1921; its Civilian Conservation Corps development began in 1933 with Minnesota’s first operating CCC state park camp. The resulting buildings use log construction and Rustic design. Two historic districts preserve different parts of that work: the service yard on Sandwick Lake and a group on Coon Lake that includes a shelter pavilion, naturalist’s cabin, water tower and stone steps. The National Park Service also prepared the park’s landscape design.
moments.notice: Log buildings and stone steps are part of the park’s CCC work.

moments.title: Marcell
moments.text: Marcell’s town center moved to meet the railway. Founded as Turtle Lake in 1905, the community changed its name the following year because other places already used it. The new name honored Andy Marcell, a Minneapolis and Rainy River Railway conductor involved in a local railway accident. In 1910, the center shifted from John Lundeen’s store on Big Turtle Lake to its present location near the tracks. Marcell lies within the Chippewa National Forest, 28 miles north of Grand Rapids. Highways 38 and 286 are now two of the community’s main routes.

moments.title: Forest History Center
moments.text: A reconstructed logging camp and an original fire tower tell different parts of the forest story at Grand Rapids’s Forest History Center. The camp re-creates 1900, with a bunkhouse, cook house, blacksmith shop and horse barn. The 100-foot tower was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1934 and moved here. The forest service cabin and tool shed are reproductions of buildings used by patrolmen and firefighting crews in the 1930s. Beside the Mississippi, a replica floating cook shack and bunkhouse recalls the river drivers who moved logs downstream to mills.
